hypothesis: An adversary who compromised Windows hosts in this network stole credentials from them (MITRE ATT&CK tactic: Credential Access).

assessments.reason: Signed Store app, crashed and produced WER reports.
PyInstaller payload pushed by PsExec from scranton as pbeesly, spawned PowerShell and dropped Rar/sdelete.
Password-protected re-archive of harvested working.zip, then deleted with sdelete.
Anti-forensics wiping Rar.exe and staged archives.
Recon tool run by pbeesly PowerShell, likely checking LSASS/registry permissions.
Lateral movement to NASHUA with cleartext pbeesly password to run python.exe.
Wiped the .scr loader, Draft.Zip and SysinternalsSuite.zip on scranton.
Masqueraded screen-saver loader launched from ProgramData by explorer, later sdelete-wiped.
Compiled in-memory payloads from the steganographic monkey.png loader into temp DLLs.
Launched with -verb runas by PowerShell, likely UAC/elevation attempt.
UAC-bypass-capable binary spawned three times by cmd under pbeesly.

frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network harvested credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: LSASS memory access by non-standard processes, SAM/NTDS.dit or registry hive reads, credential-dumping tool execution (e.g., Mimikatz, procdump on lsass), suspicious access to DPAPI secrets or browser credential stores, and subsequent authentication with harvested accounts.
frame.what_would_refute: No process access to LSASS or credential stores, no dumping tool artifacts or hive copies, and no anomalous authentication using accounts whose credentials reside on the affected hosts.

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: No dumping tooling or hive copies executed, but pbeesly is running a full hands-on-keyboard intrusion on scranton/nashua (malicious .scr, Sysinternals, sdelete, persistence, exfil, PsExec with cleartext password) and holds SeDebugPrivilege, so dumping capability was present.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: wsmprovhost as pbeesly opened lsass with 0x1f3fff on nashua.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: Only SAM_SERVER/SAM_DOMAIN handle requests are from lsass.exe itself as SCRANTON$ (S-1-5-18); no reg save, hive writes or external SAM access.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow/ntds command lines, no .dit file writes, no matching script blocks.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: No SECURITY/Policy\Secrets object access, no reg save of SECURITY, no matching script blocks; only routine CredentialGuard/CredentialEnrollmentManager registry writes.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: No SECURITY/Cache object access or cache/dcc script blocks; the credential theft seen was certificate private-key export and keystroke logging, which fall outside this sub-technique.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No dcsync/lsadump/drsuapi activity, no replication-related service installs; only PSEXESVC and a Java support service were installed.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: Only capture-related activity is netsh.exe 'trace start capture=yes' / 'trace stop' on scranton.dmevals.local, spawned by the legitimate Microsoft Azure Network Watcher agent service (NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service) running as SYSTEM, lasting ~7 seconds. No pktmon/windump/tcpdump/rawcap/tshark/Wireshark executions, no pcap/npcap/winpcap service installs, no capture driver loads, no PowerShell capture tooling, and Zeek shows only normal enterprise traffic. Consistent with cloud network-monitoring, not adversary sniffing.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: Input capture tooling (Keystroke-Check/Get-Keystrokes, Invoke-ScreenCapture, steganographic IEX loader) executed by pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local; remaining LSASS/SAM handle activity is benign Azure/system baseline.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: Get-Keystrokes job started, viewed and removed on SCRANTON at 03:06:59-03:07:49 UTC, preceded by an AV-evasion Keystroke-Check process enumeration.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: Invoke-ScreenCapture loop using System.Windows.Forms/System.Drawing captured the virtual screen to .bmp files in pbeesly's Downloads (gwq4xdwv.s5g.bmp).

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: PowerShell.exe opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF on SCRANTON and wsmprovhost.exe with 0x1F3FFF on NASHUA, consistent with credential memory access; no hooking DLL was observed, so suspicious rather than confirmed.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA interception artifacts in any dataset. All credential-provider, smart-card, biometric and Windows Hello DLLs loaded (event.code 7) are Microsoft-signed (win.Signature='Microsoft Windows', win.Signed=true), including CredProv2faHelper.dll, ngccredprov.dll, SmartcardCredentialProvider.dll, BioCredProv.dll, wlidcredprov.dll, vaultcli.dll and cryptngc.dll. LogonUI registry writes on scranton.dmevals.local were made by the legitimate C:\windows\system32\LogonUI.exe and point to the built-in password provider {60B78E88-EAD8-445C-9CFD-0B87F74EA6CD}. No 4624 used a smart-card/certificate authentication package and no MFA-related account names appeared. The 4648 events are PsExec (C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe) and Windows-internal processes using the pbeesly password, and the 7045 services are PSEXESVC and a Java support service - none are credential-provider/MFA mechanisms. The credential-related activity present (plaintext password in the Invoke-Exfil script, LSASS access by PowerShell.exe/wsmprovhost.exe) belongs to credential dumping/exfiltration, not T1111.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: PowerShell Invoke-Exfil on scranton.dmevals.local (user pbeesly) mapped \\192.168.0.4\webdav with New-PSDrive and copied OfficeSupplies.7z there; zeek shows the WebDAV redirector (DavClnt / Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir) doing OPTIONS/PROPFIND/LOCK/PUT/PROPPATCH with 401 challenges and 201/204 success to 192.168.0.4:80, and the host produced the dataset's only NTLM network logon (4624 type 3, NtLmSsp, NTLM V2, workstation 10.0.1.4).

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: Attacker-controlled PowerShell on scranton (stego loader from monkey.png, PID 2976) and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua (remote PowerShell as pbeesly) opened lsass.exe with 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff and call traces lacking any signed dump utility, indicating in-memory access to LSASS. However no dump/credential-extraction step (procdump/comsvcs/MiniDump/sekurlsa, 4688 or 4104) was observed, so exploitation for credential access is suspected but not proven; remaining LSASS opens are benign baseline (svchost, Azure agents, boot processes).

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: No process other than Microsoft Edge's own components (MicrosoftEdge.exe, MicrosoftEdgeSH.exe, MicrosoftEdgeCP.exe), svchost.exe and Explorer.EXE touched any browser cookie/credential store; the only cookie-related artifacts were Edge's DataStore\_TempTestAccess.txt and a LocalService INetCookies package directory. No injection into browser processes and no script referencing cookie databases. The malicious activity on scranton.dmevals.local was certificate export, screen capture and WebDAV exfiltration of Downloads (OfficeSupplies.7z), not web session cookie theft.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: Compromised pbeesly account ran an offensive PowerShell toolkit on SCRANTON and used WinRM to NASHUA; PowerShell.exe (0x1FFFFF/0x1F3FFF) and wsmprovhost.exe (0x1F3FFF) opened LSASS for credential/ticket extraction.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: LSASS full-access reads provide the KRBTGT hash needed for golden tickets, but all 4768/4769 events were successful AES256 with pre-auth and no forged TGT was observed.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: All 4769 service-ticket requests were normal successful AES256 requests for machine accounts and pbeesly; no forged service ticket was observed.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: pbeesly requested a TGS for the krbtgt service (Ticket Options 0x60810010) on the DC and LSASS ticket material was read on SCRANTON/NASHUA, but no RC4 downgrade or kerberoast tooling strings were seen.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: All AS-REQ events used PreAuthType 2 with AES256; no pre-auth-disabled account, no AS-REP roasting tooling or script content.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: SCRANTON: pbeesly ran a steganographic PowerShell loader (monkey.png -> IEX), stored an encoded payload in HKLM\SOFTWARE\Javasoft\value Supplement and re-executed it, and PowerShell opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff access at 03:05:16 — credential theft enabling forged-credential use; stolen creds then used for PSEXESVC lateral movement to nashua/newyork.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: Cookie/Login Data file writes were only svchost.exe and MicrosoftEdge.exe system activity; the sole 'token/cookie' PowerShell hit was the Get-AttributesMask Windows access-token helper. No browser cookie theft or forged cookie material.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: 4624 LogonProcessName/AuthenticationPackageName values are all standard (Kerberos/Advapi/User32/NtLmSsp, Kerberos/Negotiate/NTLM); SAML/NotOnOrAfter/token-signing PowerShell search returned zero hits.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No MFA request generation activity in any dataset. The only hit check (C307, event.code:7045) resolved to a Java VM support service install on scranton and repeated PSEXESVC installs on nashua (Sysinternals PsExec remote service), not MFA-fatigue tooling. PowerShell 4104 blocks contained no MFA/2FA/authenticator/Okta/Duo strings (0 rows), sysmon process creation had no MFA-related command lines (only Windows PushToInstall/dmwappushservice 'push' matches), sysmon network events showed no connections to authentication/MFA hostnames (0 rows), and windows.security contains no 4625 failed logons at all. Credential-access-adjacent activity (PsExec with cleartext password, archive staging of *pass*/*login* files) is present but is not T1621.

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: SystemCertificates write on nashua by pbeesly session.

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly (SID ...-1107) ran a PowerShell keylogging session on 2020-05-02 between 03:06:47 and 03:07:49 UTC. A 'Keystroke-Check' function was defined that enumerates running processes to detect AV products (avp, acs, outpost, mcvsescn, mcods, navapsvc, kav, AvastSvc, AvastUi, nod32krn, nod32, ekern, dwengine, MsMpEng, msseces, ekrn, savservice, scfservice, savadminservice) — classic keylogger anti-analysis. It was then invoked, followed by 'Get-Keystrokes;Start-Sleep -Seconds 15;View-Job -JobName "Keystrokes"', a second View-Job of the Keystrokes job, and Remove-Job -Name "Keystrokes" -Force to clean up. The same session also ran Invoke-ScreenCapture (screenshot loop saving .bmp to Downloads, confirmed by a file-create of C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\gwq4xdwv.s5g.bmp) and a steganography loader that decoded and IEX'd a payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png. This is interactive input capture on a compromised host.

findings.title: Invoke-ScreenCapture GUI/screen capture loop on SCRANTON
findings.summary: In the same pbeesly PowerShell session on scranton.dmevals.local, a function Invoke-ScreenCapture was defined that uses System.Windows.Forms.SystemInformation::VirtualScreen and System.Drawing.Graphics::CopyFromScreen to grab the full virtual screen every 300 seconds and save it as a randomly named .bmp in $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads. It was invoked with 'Invoke-ScreenCapture;Start-Sleep -Seconds 3;View-Job -JobName "Screenshot"', and Sysmon recorded the resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\gwq4xdwv.s5g.bmp written by powershell.exe at 03:06:00 UTC. Capturing the GUI is how an operator harvests on-screen credentials/input; no fake credential prompt (CredUIPromptForCredentials/Get-Credential) was observed, so this is GUI capture rather than a credential dialog.

findings.title: WebDAV/UNC path used by Invoke-Exfil to force NTLM authentication and exfiltrate a 7z archive to 192.168.0.4
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly, a PowerShell scriptblock (ScriptBlockId b2b03a9c-43f0-4285-837d-f22d4600b2ae, logged 2020-05-02T03:08:02Z, path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1) defines function Invoke-Exfil. It compresses the user's Downloads into $env:APPDATA\OfficeSupplies.7z with password 'lolol', builds a PSCredential for user 'cozy', then maps a drive to the UNC/WebDAV path \\192.168.0.4\webdav via New-PSDrive and copies OfficeSupplies.7z there with Copy-Item. The WebDAV redirector (Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362, DavClnt) then performs the HTTP WebDAV conversation to 192.168.0.4:80 from 10.0.1.4 — OPTIONS, PROPFIND, LOCK, PUT, PROPPATCH on /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z, with repeated 401 challenges answered and final 201/204 success — i.e. the host is coerced into authenticating to an attacker-controlled WebDAV endpoint, the forced-authentication pattern of T1187. The same host also produced a single NTLM network logon (4624 type 3, NtLmSsp, NTLM V2, target pbeesly, workstation 10.0.1.4, source 172.18.39.2) at 2020-05-02T03:20:41Z, the only NTLM logon in the whole security dataset (all other 217 type-3 logons are Kerberos). Supporting context: PowerShell created C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp\hostui.lnk at 03:04:23Z and later ran 'Start-Process C:\Windows\System32\hostui.exe -verb runas' (03:21:26Z); PSEXESVC services were installed on nashua.dmevals.local by pbeesly. The zeek window (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window, so the WebDAV flows are the network-side record of the same tooling rather than a time-correlated match.

findings.summary: The remaining T1187 check hits are normal system behaviour. All 66 outbound SMB (445/139) connections in windows.sysmon are generated by process.executable 'System' (the kernel SMB client) under user SYSTEM, going to 10.0.0.4 (26), the link-local address fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429 (24) and 10.0.1.6 (16) — ordinary file-server/DFS traffic, not coercion. The two .lnk files under C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Recent\ were created by C:\windows\Explorer.EXE at 2020-05-02T02:58:44Z, which is Explorer's normal Recent-items behaviour, not a lure. The 5140/5145 share access is limited to SYSVOL, IPC$ and ADMIN$ (domain administration), and the 4663/4656 object types are overwhelmingly registry Keys. The zeek SMB flows (45 to 445, 5 to 139) are likewise plain conn records. Note the only genuinely malicious shortcut is the StartUp hostui.lnk created by PowerShell, reported in the malicious finding.

Of 326 Sysmon event.code 10 records targeting lsass.exe, 289 came from C:\windows\system32\svchost.exe (286 at GrantedAccess 0x1000, 2 at 0x101001, 1 at 0x3000), 15 from C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.Security.IaaSAntimalware\1.5.5.9\AntimalwareConfig.exe and 13 from C:\WindowsAzure\Packages\Telemetry\WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe (0x1000/0x1400) — standard AV/telemetry query rights. The wininit.exe (0x1000000, 0x1fffff), csrss.exe (0x1fffff) and services.exe (0x1000) opens all occur at 03:19:09-03:19:13 on scranton, matching a boot/restart sequence (lsass.exe itself was created at 03:19:09.809 by wininit.exe). No service ticket was presented for a service whose account hash was demonstrably extracted, and no anomalous service-account logons appeared. No browser cookie store was read or modified by the malicious PowerShell chain, and no forged cookie material was written. The credential access observed on SCRANTON was LSASS memory access, not cookie forgery.
